title: How Language Models Work
description: The vocabulary you need to read about, argue about and use a language model well.

cards.front: The unit a language model actually reads and writes — usually a word piece, not a word
cards.note: Roughly ¾ of a word in English on average; rarer words and other scripts cost more tokens.

cards.front: The total amount of text a model can attend to at once, prompt and reply together
cards.note: Anything outside it does not exist for the model: it is not forgotten, it was never there.

cards.front: A confident statement that is simply not true, produced because it was plausible text
cards.note: The model optimises for likely continuations, not for verified ones, so plausibility is the failure mode.

cards.front: Giving a model examples of the task inside the prompt instead of retraining it
cards.note: Zero-shot is asking with no examples at all; both change behaviour without changing weights.

cards.front: Fetching relevant documents and putting them in the prompt before answering
cards.note: It grounds an answer in sources the model did not memorise, and lets you cite them.

cards.front: The setting that controls how much randomness there is in the next-token choice
cards.note: Near zero is repeatable and flat; higher is more varied and more likely to wander.

cards.front: Continuing to train a finished model on your own examples to specialise it
Training that uses people's preferences between answers as the reward signal
cards.back: RLHF — reinforcement learning from human feedback

cards.front: The architecture behind essentially every modern language model
cards.note: Its trick is attention: every token can look at every other token in the window.

cards.front: The mechanism that lets a model weigh which earlier tokens matter for the next one
Asking a model to work through the steps before giving the answer
cards.note: It measurably helps on multi-step problems — the intermediate tokens are where the work happens.

cards.front: Text placed above the conversation that sets the model's role and rules
Input crafted to make a model ignore its instructions and follow the input instead
cards.note: The reason anything a model reads — a web page, a file, an email — is data, never orders.

cards.front: A number vector that places a piece of text near others with similar meaning
cards.note: Semantic search is nearest-neighbour lookup over embeddings.

cards.front: The date after which a model has seen nothing at all
cards.note: It is why a model can be fluent about a topic and still be a year out of date on it.

cards.front: Giving a model tools it can call — search, code, a database — instead of answering from memory
Taking the next token only from the smallest set whose probabilities add up to a threshold
cards.note: It cuts the long tail of unlikely tokens without fixing the count, unlike top-k.

cards.front: The rough rule that bigger models trained on more data get predictably better
Why a model miscounts how many times a given character appears in a word
cards.note: The word may arrive as one or two chunks, with no spelling inside them.

cards.front: The safest assumption about anything a model tells you that matters
cards.note: Fluency is not evidence. The model is a strong first draft and a poor last word.
